newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN CURRENCY BOARD SEEN STABILISING ECONOMY.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN CURRENCY BOARD SEEN STABILISING ECONOMY.

text.p: Bulgaria's government and central bank have accepted an International Monetary Fund proposal for a currency board to stabilise the economy and halt the fall in the lev.
Details of how the board would work and what exchange rate would be used have not yet been settled but some outlines are already known.

Under the scheme, expected to be introduced early next year for an indefinite period, levs in circulation and commercial banks' mimimum reserves deposited at the central bank must be exactly matched with central bank foreign exchange and gold reserves.
Economists say the IMF is unlikely to support introducing a board at a very devalued lev rate as this would be inflationary.
Currency boards, effectively pegging the local currency usually to the dollar, have been used by countries like Argentina, Lithuania and Estonia to restore confidence and defeat hyperinflation.
Bulgaria's parliament would have yet to debate on whether to peg the lev to the dollar or the mark.

The dollar is widely perceived as a benchmark of stability and most people convert savings into dollars. Germany, however, is Bulgaria's biggest investor and trade partner and in view of Bulgaria's association accord with the European Union, the mark could also be appropriate.

The cabinet last week proposed operating the currency board from the central bank by dividing the bank into two departments, one of which would act as a currency board and the other one as a banking department.
Critics of the mechanism express concern at how it will be supervised, and say it does not address the problem of Bulgaria's domestic debt, which reached 668 billion levs at end-October.
The IMF had proposed rolling over maturity payments until interest rates fall under the effect of the currency board.
But finance ministry officials doubt whether financial institutions struggling to operate under the austere currency board system would be able to buy government sucurities at all.
Some economists have warned a currency board could lead to more closures of illiquid banks as it would halt commercial bank refinancing.

However this may depend on what version of the board is adopted. Under a softer currency board plan, the central bank's banking supervision department could still provide limited refinancing to commercial banks.
The IMF says the markets for government securities and for foreign exchange would continue to function normally.

"In fact, the stability of financial markets under a currency board would likely result in an increase in confidence in the securities market," said a statement from the IMF resident mission in Sofia.
